options.label: Rarefaction
options.summary: Repeated subsampling to a common depth. Discards reads and excludes shallow samples.

options.label: CSS scaling
options.summary: Cumulative sum scaling. Keeps every sample, assumes a shared scaling regime.

options.label: CLR transform
options.summary: Centered log-ratio. Compositionally rigorous, needs a zero-replacement rule.

note.message: CLR (Aitchison) is the default for this run. Rarefaction at any defensible depth would exclude 139/148 samples (retaining only 9, or 6.1%), which violates the retention-floor rule: rarefying away more than half the cohort is not a defensible default. CLR preserves all 148 samples and treats sequencing data as compositional by construction. Differential abundance will use unrarefied counts with method-specific normalization in Step 7; alpha/beta diversity metrics will use CLR-transformed values and Aitchison distance.

positions.claim: Rarefaction, when repeated subsampling is conducted with sufficient iterations, provides robust control of sequencing-depth effects on alpha and beta diversity metrics by equalizing sampling effort across all samples.

Rarefying discards valid sequence data and inflates variance to match the smallest library size, making it statistically inadmissible for differential abundance and reducing power for taxon-level testing, particularly when information loss is severe.

Sequencing data are compositional by construction (constrained to sum to sequencing depth), making log-ratio transformations such as CLR/Aitchison the statistically principled solution throughout the pipeline, rather than selecting a single global depth that fits no analysis equally well.

g1.note_message: DiseaseState is the only candidate likely_outcome column and directly specifies a binary biological comparison. The column name unambiguously indicates health status (H = healthy, PAR = parasite-associated or parasitic disease), and the balanced counts (74 vs. 74 samples) confirm a deliberate case-control design. No alternative grouping variable exists.

g2.note_message: No usable technical/batch column was classified in the provided metadata. The paperclip literature retrieval system is not available to obtain the original paper's real description of sequencing-run allocation. Therefore, no real citation for batch handling can be provided at this time.

g3.note_message: Each of the 148 samples represents a distinct subject with no repeated observations (repeated_subjects = 0). The unit of inference is the independent sample. Downstream inference should use standard independent-sample methods that do not assume clustering or pairing.

recommendation.label: RECOMMENDS GENUS
recommendation.rationale: This dataset yields 114 genus-level features with reasonable completeness, representing a well-supported intermediate resolution. The progression from 10 phyla to 40 families to 114 genera shows no collapse or sparsity warning at genus level. Genus provides substantially finer biological interpretation than the coarser family (40 features) or phylum (10 features) ranks while remaining statistically practical and matching the standard reporting rank for short-read 16S markers in the literature.

note.message: Alpha-diversity inference uses α=0.05 (two-sided) with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control across the three primary metrics (observed richness, Shannon, Simpson). This run compares two groups (Healthy [H]=74, Parkinson [PAR]=74) as independent samples. The rarefaction depth step will retain 9 samples post-filtering, which is extremely small and creates a severe caveat: power is vastly reduced, and any inference depends critically on whether the 139 excluded samples were balanced by group. Critically: this 94% sample exclusion rate is a red flag. The BH correction is scoped to the alpha-diversity metric family only and is not pooled with the hundreds of differential-abundance tests downstream.

Bray-Curtis (abundance-weighted) is the conventional primary metric for genus-level 16S analysis with rarefaction normalization and no phylogenetic tree. This run used rarefaction (G6) rather than CLR transformation, making Bray-Curtis the appropriate metric for detecting shifts in taxon abundances. The analysis includes two independent groups (H: 74 samples, PAR: 74 samples) with 68.8% sparsity. Jaccard (presence/absence) remains available as a sensitivity check to detect community membership changes not captured by abundance. UniFrac is unavailable—no phylogenetic tree exists for this project's data, so phylogenetic distance metrics cannot be computed.

10% prevalence filter applied. This run retains 63 genera at the 10% threshold, down from 115 at 0% and 72 at 5%; moving to 20% removes only 14 more, indicating that most surviving taxa have moderate prevalence. With balanced groups (H=74, PAR=74) and 148 total samples, the 10% policy reduces testing burden from 115 to 63 features (~45% retention) while preserving genera detected in ≥15 samples overall—a standard defensible threshold in DA benchmarking. The sensitivity analysis uses a single transparent method (CLR transformation + Wilcoxon rank-sum), not a multi-method consensus, so robustness is assessed by effect stability and prevalence inspection rather than method agreement.

synthesis.hero_finding: Severe sample retention loss (9 of 148 retained; only ~4–5 per group after rarefaction at depth 4200) compromises inference; within the retained subset, one genus was significantly enriched in the PAR group with modest community-level compositional shift, but canonical CRC-associated taxa were absent or filtered.
synthesis.summary_text: This analysis retained only 9 of 148 samples following rarefaction at 4200 reads, leaving approximately 4–5 samples per group. Within this severely depleted dataset, alpha diversity metrics were largely stable between groups (Shannon p=0.056, n.s. after correction), and beta diversity showed a statistically significant but modest compositional shift (PERMANOVA R²=0.019, p=0.019, driven by modest unequal dispersion rather than a large community-level reordering). At the genus level, a single taxon reached significance (q=0.027, enriched in PAR, 98.6% prevalence), whereas literature-expected CRC-associated genera (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas) were either dropped by the 10% prevalence filter or undetected. Canonical butyrate-producing genera (Roseburia, Faecalibacterium) showed direction consistent with prior CRC studies but did not reach significance.
synthesis.literature_validation_text: Expected CRC-associated taxa from cross-cohort metagenomic studies were either filtered or absent, preventing direct literature replication of known markers. Butyrate-producing genera (Roseburia, Faecalibacterium) showed the expected enrichment in controls consistent with disease-association meta-analyses, but the severely reduced sample size prevented robust confirmation of these associations. The inability to detect canonical dysbiosis markers may reflect either genuine absence in this cohort, loss during rarefaction to accommodate shallow samples, or cohort-specific differences; it cannot be disambiguated given the data retention crisis.

limitations.title: Catastrophic sample-size loss
limitations.body: Rarefaction at 4200 reads retained only 9 of 148 samples (~6% retention), leaving approximately 4–5 samples per group. This destroys statistical power for all comparisons; any p-values reported here should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating only, not confirmatory. The extreme exclusion imbalance introduces selection bias: excluded samples may differ systematically from retained ones in composition, disease severity, or sequencing quality.

limitations.title: Genus-level 16S resolution
limitations.body: 16S rRNA taxonomy at the genus rank cannot discriminate species or strain-level variation. If CRC-associated signal is concentrated in a specific species within a genus (e.g., Fusobacterium nucleatum vs. other Fusobacterium spp.), this assay cannot detect it. Conversely, oppositely-associated species within the same genus may cancel out, producing a null result despite real dysbiosis.

limitations.title: Cross-sectional design cannot establish causality
limitations.body: Association between taxon abundance and PAR status does not imply the taxon drives disease, prevents disease, or is merely a biomarker of another causal process. Temporal, intervention, or mechanistic studies are required to infer directionality.

limitations.title: Single DA method; no multi-method consensus
limitations.body: Differential abundance was tested by CLR normalization + Wilcoxon rank-sum only. Alternative robust methods (ANCOM-BC2, ALDEx2) were unavailable in this pipeline. A single positive result cannot be validated against method agreement, limiting confidence in the robustness of the single significant hit.

limitations.title: Missing taxon identity in primary DA result
limitations.body: The single significantly differentially abundant genus is not named in the results table, preventing biological interpretation or literature contextualization of this finding. This is a data reporting gap that must be resolved before the result can be meaningfully discussed.

next_steps.title: Specificity check via CDI dataset
next_steps.hypothesis: The single significantly enriched taxon in PAR is a marker of general dysbiosis (enriched across multiple disease contexts) rather than a CRC-specific signature.
next_steps.experiment: Re-analyze the C. difficile infection (CDI) dataset (cdi_schubert) using identical preprocessing and DA methods (CLR + Wilcoxon, same prevalence threshold). If the same taxon is significantly enriched in CDI cases, it is unlikely to be CRC-specific; if absent or depleted in CDI cases, it may be more CRC-associated. This discriminates general dysbiosis markers from disease-specific ones without requiring new samples.

next_steps.title: Sample-recovery and re-rarefaction sensitivity
next_steps.hypothesis: The extreme rarefaction depth (4200 reads) was necessary to accommodate shallow samples but discarded much usable data; a less stringent rarefaction depth (e.g., 2500–3500 reads) or alternative normalization (CLR without rarefaction) could recover samples and statistical power without sacrificing biological meaning.
next_steps.experiment: Retrieve the full (unrarefied) count table and re-run the complete pipeline at shallower rarefaction depths (e.g., 2500, 3000, 3500) while tracking sample retention and effect-size stability for alpha, beta, and DA. If alpha, beta, and the DA hit remain qualitatively consistent across rarefaction depths, confidence in the finding increases; if they change substantially, the result is fragile. This test should be done before interpreting the single DA hit or investing in external validation.

next_steps.title: Identify and validate single DA taxon
next_steps.hypothesis: The single significantly enriched taxon in PAR represents a genuine disease-associated signal; if species-level identity can be resolved, targeted qPCR or strain-specific sequencing may confirm its presence and role.
next_steps.experiment: First, retrieve the taxon name from the full results table (this is a data reporting prerequisite). Then, search the literature for prior reports of this genus in colorectal disease, dysbiosis, or the specimen type used (stool/biopsy/etc.). If prior evidence exists and is consistent with the literature-expected direction (enriched in cases, not healthy controls), proceed to species-level or strain-level resolution via shotgun metagenomics or targeted 16S amplicon sequencing on the excluded/shallow samples or on a prospectively collected independent CRC cohort.

next_steps.title: Investigate rarefaction-driven loss of canonical markers
next_steps.hypothesis: The absence of Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, and Porphyromonas reflects genuine ecological absence rather than filtering or sequencing-depth artifacts in this specific cohort.
next_steps.experiment: Examine the raw (pre-rarefaction) prevalence and abundance distribution of the four canonical CRC-associated genera in the full dataset. If they are present in the full data but dropped by the 10% prevalence threshold or lost to rarefaction, recalculate what threshold would have retained them and whether lowering the prevalence threshold materially changes the DA results or introduces instability (sign of overfitting). If they are genuinely rare/absent even in raw counts, this suggests either true cohort heterogeneity (disease stage, antibiotic exposure, or geographic/population differences) or misclassification of the PAR group.
